extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and readers interested in publication ethics and academic integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for academic (mathematical) journal articles, focusing on peer review, editorial oversight, plagiarism checks, and appropriate scholarly content. Includes expectations for publishers' processes (audits, retractions, accessibility) and reviewer/editor accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contains scientific content
rubrics_metrics.description: An article must contain genuine scientific/mathematical content; papers that 'contain no scientific content' should be retracted or rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notice: 'This article has been retracted ... as the article contains no scientific content and was accepted because of an administrative error.' The abstract and conclusions must be meaningful and substantively advance knowledge; nonsensical abstracts/conclusions (e.g., 'a problematic problem') are unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper peer review prior to acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance decisions must be based on documented, genuine peer review rather than administrative errors or absent review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece was 'accepted because of an administrative error' and readers question how it 'get past editors, peer reviewers, and publication staffs.' Journals should ensure an actual peer review occurred before acceptance and record the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial preliminary screening / sanity check
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should perform a rapid preliminary scan to detect obviously unsuitable, incoherent, or fraudulent submissions and reject them without wasting reviewers' time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an editor commented: 'When I get a paper I make a precursory scan... If it is clear that the paper is unsuitable ... I immediately reject the paper to not even waste a reviewer’s time.' 'Anybody could tell in 5 seconds that the paper on question is a fraud.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism and similarity checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions must be screened for plagiarism and overlap against journals and web content using similarity-detection software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor Leszek Demkowicz: 'We have now a new system in place within which each submission is carefully checked using Elsevier provided software against practically everything: our own journal, other Elsevier journals, other journals and even web pages…' Several comments note verbatim copying from web pages (e.g., cut-the-knot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate, scholarly references
rubrics_metrics.description: References should cite relevant scholarly literature; citing irrelevant web pages, games sites, or non-scholarly sources is a red flag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments point out references to sites that 'sell mathematical games (e.g. cut-the-knot.org)' and many papers were nearly identical and cited random books and URLs rather than appropriate scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify authors' identities and affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should verify that author contact information and affiliations are legitimate and not bogus or informal email addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns raised about an author using a 'budweiser.com' email address and other signs suggesting the authorship/affiliation information may be unreliable; verification can detect prank or fraudulent submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful handling of author-suggested reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: If author-suggested reviewers are used, journals must independently vet them to prevent fake or friendly reviewers from subverting review integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: journals ask authors for potential reviewers (up to 8), which can enable close friends or fake identities. 'Those can be close friends, and who knows, even the main author himself behind a fake email address.' Vet suggested reviewers carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer independence and competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must be independent, qualified in the paper's topic, and free from conflicts; editors must avoid selecting only 'friendly' reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments note editors can 'select friendly reviewers' and thereby bypass scrutiny. Ensure reviewers have relevant expertise and are not simply 'peers' in the social sense; verify competence and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher/journal auditing of review processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should periodically audit peer review processes—sample review files, contact reviewers, and check that procedures were followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested publisher quality control: 'routinely sampling the review processes, selecting a few papers and: a) Looking at the reviews. b) Contacting the reviewers and asking them to comment on the process.' This can detect misuse by editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction notices should be openly accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices and the reasons for retraction should be publicly accessible and not hidden behind paywalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters objected that retractions or the retracted paper required payment to view; 'Retractions should never be behind a paywall.' Open retraction notices aid transparency and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial accountability and complaints procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be formal mechanisms to investigate and discipline editors and to handle complaints, e.g., following COPE flowcharts and journal appeals procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters call for holding editors accountable. Karen Shashok: 'Before you contact COPE with a complaint you should go through the journal’s own complaints or appeals procedure... COPE just posted a revised flowchart ... to explain how they now handle complaints against editors.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient domain expertise among production staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Production and editorial staff should have enough subject-matter knowledge (or access to such expertise) to spot obvious problems in submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculation that 'production staffs may not have the domain expertise' and thus may miss glaringly unsuitable manuscripts; publishers should ensure staff can detect discipline-specific red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate, qualified reviewer pool
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals need a sufficient number of unpaid, qualified volunteer reviewers to ensure rigorous evaluation and prevent overreliance on a small group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment: 'we need even more journals for unpaid, under-appreciated and insufficient number of volunteer reviewers to steer the course of science.' A larger, diverse reviewer pool reduces risk of collusion and oversight failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent and robust editorial response to misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: When misconduct is detected, editors/publishers should respond transparently (clear notices, retraction where appropriate) and communicate findings publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect a substantive 'mea culpa' and visible corrective action. Comments stress editors should 'send a strong message, “we're onto you”' and that publishers should not obscure retractions or limit access to the rationale.
